title.en: Transportation in Plants and Circulation in Animals

text.en: Meena watched a coloured flower take up inked water. "Water travels up the stem," said her teacher.

Materials move in cells by diffusion, from higher to lower concentration, by osmosis, the movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane, and by active transport, which uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient. Root hairs take in water and minerals.
Water moves across the root by the apoplast and symplast pathways, and it rises in xylem mainly because of transpiration pull and water cohesion, with root pressure contributing in some conditions, which is the ascent of sap. Transpiration is loss of water vapour from leaves. Phloem translocates sugars from sources such as mature leaves to sinks where sugars are used or stored.
In the human circulatory system blood circulates in blood vessels, which are arteries carrying blood away from the heart, veins bringing it back and capillaries joining them. The heart pumps the blood, and the chapter describes blood, the heart's working and lymph.

text.en: Water can cross the root through cell walls and through connected cells. It rises in xylem mainly due to transpiration pull and water cohesion. Root pressure can also contribute.

text.en: Transpiration is loss of water vapour from leaves.

board.text: transpiration pull

text.en: Phloem carries dissolved sugars from sources, such as mature leaves, to sinks that use or store them, such as roots, fruits or growing shoots.

board.text: phloem transport

text.en: In the human circulatory system, arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins bring blood back. Capillary networks link the small vessels and exchange substances with tissues.

board.text: arteries and veins

text.en: The heart pumps the blood, and the chapter describes blood, the heart's working and lymph.

board.text: diffusion

text.en: If more particles are present on one side of a space, random motion tends to spread them out. The net movement is from the higher concentration to the lower concentration.

board.text: Diffusion moves particles down a concentration gradient

text.en: Water can pass across a selectively permeable membrane. In a simple model, it moves overall towards the side with more dissolved material when other conditions match.

board.text: Osmosis is the net movement of water

text.en: Root cells can take up some mineral ions even when their concentration is already higher inside the cell. Energy helps move the ions against the concentration gradient.

board.text: Active transport needs cellular energy

text.en: Long, narrow root hairs increase the surface that touches moist soil. Water enters across their membranes and mineral ions can also be taken up.

board.text: Root hairs increase contact with the soil

text.en: The apoplast pathway crosses cell walls and spaces outside membranes. The symplast pathway runs through the connected interiors of cells.

board.text: Apoplast and symplast are two pathways

text.en: A waterproof strip blocks the wall-only route around endodermal cells. Water and dissolved materials that reach that barrier must cross a cell membrane.

board.text: The endodermis controls passage into the xylem

text.en: Water entering xylem can reach the stem and leaves. The transport of this water upwards is called the ascent of sap.

board.text: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals

text.en: Evaporation from leaves creates a pull on the water in xylem. Water molecules attract each other, which helps maintain a continuous column.

board.text: Transpiration draws water upwards

text.en: Dissolved ions in the xylem can draw water in. The incoming water creates pressure that can push some water upwards.

board.text: Root pressure can help move water

text.en: Moving dry air can carry water vapour away from a leaf more quickly. In humid air there is less difference between the leaf and the surrounding air.

board.text: Wind and humidity can change transpiration

text.en: A mature leaf can supply sugars. A fruit, storage root or growing shoot can receive them. Which part is a source can change as a plant grows.

board.text: Phloem moves sugars from sources to sinks

text.en: Plasma carries water and dissolved materials. Blood cells and platelets travel within it.

board.text: Blood contains cells and plasma

text.en: The haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen. White blood cells are involved in defence, and platelets help in forming blood clots.

board.text: Red cells carry oxygen and white cells help defend

text.en: Capillary walls are very thin. Oxygen and dissolved nutrients can leave the blood, while carbon dioxide and other wastes can enter it.

board.text: Capillaries allow exchanges

text.en: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart. Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood, so oxygen level does not determine the vessel name.

board.text: A vessel’s direction determines its name

text.en: The upper chambers receive blood. The lower chambers squeeze to send blood to the lungs or the rest of the body.

board.text: Atria receive blood and ventricles pump it out

text.en: The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs. After gas exchange, blood returns to the left atrium.

board.text: Pulmonary circulation goes through the lungs

text.en: The left ventricle sends blood to the body. The blood supplies tissues and returns to the right atrium.

board.text: Systemic circulation reaches the body

text.en: Follow one trip through the lungs and one through the body. The blood passes back through the heart between the two loops.

board.text: Double circulation uses two linked loops

text.en: As the heart contracts and relaxes, changing pressure opens and closes its valves. Their movement prevents significant backflow.

board.text: Valves help maintain one-way flow

text.en: A pulse is a pressure wave caused by a heartbeat. Blood pressure measures the force per unit area on the walls of blood vessels.

board.text: Blood pressure and pulse describe different things

text.en: Blood cells can carry different markers, such as those used for ABO and Rh groups. Health professionals test compatibility before transfusion.

board.text: Blood groups matter for compatibility

text.en: Some fluid leaves the capillaries. The lymphatic system collects excess fluid and returns it to the bloodstream, and lymph nodes contribute to immune defence.

board.text: Lymph returns excess tissue fluid

problem.en: Name the tissue that transports sugars in plants.

text.en: Sugars made in leaves must reach other parts.
The tissue for food transport is phloem.
This is translocation.

problem.en: Why can a root cell take up a mineral ion against its concentration gradient?

text.en: The concentration gradient favours movement in the other direction.

why.en: Simple diffusion does not account for uptake against the gradient.

text.en: Active transport uses cellular energy to help move the ion into the cell.

why.en: This allows the cell to accumulate needed minerals.

problem.en: Why does closing leaf pores often slow water rise through xylem?

text.en: Less water vapour escapes from the leaf.

why.en: Closing the pores usually reduces transpiration.

text.en: The pull on the xylem water column becomes weaker.

why.en: Transpiration is a major driver of upward water movement.

problem.en: A vessel carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Is it an artery?

text.en: Yes. It carries blood away from the heart.

why.en: The direction is the defining feature.

text.en: It is the pulmonary artery.

why.en: The blood gains oxygen later at lung capillaries.

prompt.en: A friend says Arteries bring blood back to the heart. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

points.en: Diffusion goes from high to low concentration.
